beginner: Parsley likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost worked in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. It is forgiving, but rich, steady soil keeps the leaves tender and green and feeds a plant you cut from all season. It has a deeper root than most salad greens, so loosen the bed well; hard, compacted, or waterlogged ground holds it back and invites root rot.
seasoned: Parsley grows in most soils but does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends a soil rich in organic matter and steady moisture for the long cut-and-come-again season. Work compost into the top several inches before sowing to feed the plant through the months you harvest from it, and loosen the bed deeply because parsley sends down a slender taproot. It dislikes compacted or waterlogged ground, which checks growth and invites crown and root rot.

beginner: Parsley grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota lists as best for parsley; it still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Parsley is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Parsley does not need much feeding. Mix some compost or a little balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it a light feeding once or twice over the season, since you cut from the same plants for a long time. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks because watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Parsley is a light to moderate feeder grown for steady leafy growth over a long season. The University of Minnesota suggests a 5-10-5 fertilizer at about 3 ounces per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season, on top of compost worked in before planting. Because you cut from the same plants for months, a light midseason side-dress of nitrogen keeps fresh green leaves coming; in containers a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks replaces what frequent watering leaches out. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which draws aphids and softens the flavor.

beginner: Time to give your parsley a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your parsley with a light feeding.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5 worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly once or twice during the season.
seasoned: Moderate, balanced feeding for steady leaf growth: a 5-10-5 or balanced vegetable fertilizer worked in before sowing, then a light side-dress once or twice through the season. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor and draws aphids on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding partway through the season; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.
seasoned: About 3 ounces of 5-10-5 per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a single light midseason feeding.

beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and dotted yellow-orange, chewing the leaves and stems, sometimes stripping a stalk. They are the larvae of the black swallowtail butterfly, and many gardeners leave them be.
seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes) feeding on the foliage, banded green and black with yellow spots; on parsley they are seldom numerous enough to do real damage, and parsley is one of their host plants, so most growers tolerate or relocate them rather than spray.

beginner: Big green-and-black striped caterpillars that eat the leaves. They turn into beautiful black swallowtail butterflies, so they are usually welcome guests rather than a real problem.
seasoned: The caterpillar stage of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on parsley and other carrot-family plants; populations on a home planting are normally small.

beginner: If you want every leaf, just pick the caterpillars off by hand and move them to a spare plant. They are easy to see and there are rarely many. Planting a little extra parsley lets you share with the butterflies.
seasoned: Hand-pick where leaf loss matters and relocate the larvae to a sacrificial plant; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls them if needed, but on parsley they rarely warrant it. Many gardeners deliberately grow extra parsley as a swallowtail host.

beginner: Pick them off by hand, grow a few extra plants to share, and enjoy the butterflies they become.
seasoned: Scout occasionally and hand-pick if leaf loss matters; tolerate the small numbers a home planting usually sees, and plant extra parsley as a host plant for the butterflies.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of aphids on growing tips and leaf undersides, the most common parsley pest; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Parsley's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on parsley; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse picked leaves well before use.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which the parsley umbels attract when allowed to flower.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting a second-year plant flower draws in aphid predators.

beginner: Tunnels and rusty-brown trails in the roots and lower stems, stunted or off-color plants, and grubs at the crown. These carrot-family root pests hit parsley too.
seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae) and the carrot weevil mining the taproot and crown of parsley, a carrot-family host; damage shows as rust-colored tunneling, stunting, and secondary rot, worst where Apiaceae are grown in the same ground year after year.

beginner: Small root maggots from carrot-family pests that tunnel into the parsley root and crown, leaving rusty trails and weak plants.
seasoned: The carrot rust fly and carrot weevil lay eggs near carrot-family plants; their larvae bore into the roots and crowns. They build up where carrots, parsley, and their relatives repeat in the same bed.

beginner: Cover the bed with floating row cover to keep the flies off, rotate parsley away from where carrots or parsley grew, and clean up crop debris in fall.
seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover from emergence, rotate out of Apiaceae ground on a multi-year cycle, delay sowing past the first fly generation where it is severe, and remove crop residue that harbors overwintering stages.

beginner: Use a row cover, move parsley to a fresh spot each year, and clear away old plants in fall.
seasoned: Manage by exclusion (row cover) and rotation: keep parsley out of recent carrot-family ground, time sowings around the fly's generations, and sanitize residue.

beginner: Small tan to brown spots with darker edges scattered across the leaves, sometimes with tiny dark specks in the centers, worst in wet weather. Heavily spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Numerous small circular tan-to-brown leaf lesions, often with dark pycnidia in the centers, the most commonly reported parsley disease; it spreads in cool, wet, splashy conditions and can arrive on infected seed, and on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the cutting.

beginner: A fungal leaf-spot disease, the most common one on parsley, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and can come in on the seed.
seasoned: Septoria petroselini, a seed-borne and splash-spread fungus favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. Pick and use the clean leaves promptly.
seasoned: Use clean or treated seed, water at the soil line, space for airflow, rotate away from parsley and its relatives, and remove infected debris; the home garden has no reliable spray cure once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Wilting, yellowing plants whose crown or roots have turned brown, soft, and mushy, usually in wet, poorly drained soil. Affected plants collapse and do not recover.
seasoned: Soilborne crown and root rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia, and related fungi) attacking parsley's taproot and crown in saturated, poorly drained ground; symptoms are wilting, stunting, and a browned, decayed crown, often on plants held over a wet winter.

beginner: Soil fungi rot the parsley root and crown when the soil stays too wet, especially over a soggy winter.
seasoned: Soilborne water-mold and fungal rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia) favored by waterlogged, poorly drained soil and overwatering.

beginner: There is no cure for a rotting plant, so remove it. Improve drainage, plant in raised or loosened beds, and do not overwater, especially in winter.
seasoned: Remove affected plants; manage by prevention: well-drained or raised beds, loosened soil for the taproot, moderate winter watering, and rotation out of ground where Apiaceae rotted before.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and pull any plant whose crown has gone soft and brown.
seasoned: Site in well-drained, loosened soil, avoid waterlogging (especially overwinter), and rotate away from beds with a rot history.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where parsley's slow germination leaves seed sitting for weeks.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting parsley seed sits a long time before emerging.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that prolongs parsley's already slow germination favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and soak the seed first so it comes up faster.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and soak the dry seed to shorten the vulnerable slow-germination window.

beginner: Water deeply about once a week so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; parsley has a taproot and takes moderate dry spells better than shallow greens, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long season.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is hot and dry.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in hot, dry spells; the University of Minnesota advises watering deeply at least once a week. Mulch helps hold even moisture for a crop you cut from for months.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks Septoria leaf spot and other leaf diseases on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mushy at the crown in soggy soil.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and crown or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground, especially over winter.

beginner: Wilting leaves that taste tougher and sharper, and slowed growth when the soil dries out.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tougher, sharper-tasting leaves; sustained drought stress also coarsens the foliage, though parsley recovers from short dry spells better than salad greens.

beginner: Parsley is very slow to sprout, often 2 to 5 weeks, so keep the soil surface evenly damp the whole time. Letting it dry out is the main reason parsley seed fails.
seasoned: Parsley germination is long and slow, 2 to 5 weeks, so keep the seedbed evenly moist that whole time; letting it dry mid-emergence is the classic reason a parsley stand fails.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture while they establish.

beginner: Parsley has a deep taproot, so it takes a short dry spell better than salad greens, but even water, about an inch a week deep, keeps the leaves tender and green. Water at the base and mulch to hold moisture.
seasoned: Parsley has a taproot and rides out moderate dry spells better than shallow greens, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long season; UMN advises watering deeply at least once a week. Water at the soil line against Septoria leaf spot, and mulch to hold even moisture.

beginner: Keep watering evenly through the long harvest. Parsley handles a short dry spell, but a long drought makes the leaves tough and sharp.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the long cutting season; the taproot forgives a short dry spell, but prolonged drought toughens and sharpens the leaves.

beginner: In year two parsley runs to flower and the leaves turn bitter. Ease off the water as it bolts, since the plant is finishing its life cycle.
seasoned: In its second year parsley bolts to flower and seed and the leaf quality falls off; ease off watering as it runs up, since the plant is finishing its biennial cycle.

beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender and green; parsley handles a short dry spell, but long droughts make it tough.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps parsley growing tender and green through a long season; the deeper taproot lets it ride out short dry spells, but prolonged drought toughens the leaves.

seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the long, slow germination, which can take 2 to 5 weeks, and through establishment; once the taproot is down the plant is more forgiving.

beginner: You can plant parsley straight in the garden or start it indoors. The seeds are slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks, so soak them in warm water for up to a day before planting and keep the soil moist the whole time. Sow about a quarter inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since parsley handles frost. For an earlier start, sow indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and move the young plants outside after hardening them off, while they are still small.
seasoned: Parsley can be direct-sown or started indoors. Its seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, and germinates poorly in cold soil, so soaking the dry seed in warm water for up to 24 hours before sowing speeds and evens emergence. Direct-sow about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since parsley tolerates frost. To get a head start, sow indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off; parsley moves better when young, before the taproot is long, so transplant on the early side. Keep the seedbed evenly moist through the long germination.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter, deep enough for parsley's taproot.

beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a little balanced starter fertilizer; parsley is a moderate feeder over a long season.

beginner: Parsley is hardy and a pot of it can keep going well into fall and through a mild winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since it takes frost. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes. Remember parsley is a biennial: a plant carried through winter will send up a flower stalk and turn bitter in spring, so start fresh plants each year for the best leaves.
seasoned: Parsley is a frost-hardy biennial, so a container can hold through fall and overwinter in mild zones in a sheltered spot, giving fresh leaves late and early. The limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes. Note that an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring as the leaves coarsen, so treat it as a short early-spring bonus and sow fresh plants for the main crop.

beginner: Parsley is an easy, long-lasting container herb. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep to fit its root, keep it watered, and snip the outer stems so it keeps regrowing. It does well on a sunny windowsill or step and handles cool weather, so a pot can carry on long after summer crops are done.
seasoned: Parsley grows well in a container at least 10 inches deep to fit its taproot, harvested cut-and-come-again from the outer stems. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast, and feed lightly through the long season. A pot is the easiest way to keep parsley by the kitchen door and to move a frost-hardy plant into shelter as the weather turns, extending the leaf supply into late fall and, in mild zones, winter.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits parsley well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and green over a long harvest.

beginner: Parsley has a deeper root than most herbs, so use a pot at least 10 inches deep. Extra width lets you grow more plants to cut from.
seasoned: Parsley has a slender taproot, so give it depth: a container at least 10 inches deep suits it better than a shallow tray, while width adds room for several plants to cut from.

beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley itself, dill, fennel, celery, parsnip, and cilantro. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (the carrot rust fly and carrot weevil, leafhopper-vectored aster yellows, Septoria, and soilborne crown rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow parsley or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant parsley after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Parsley left to flower in its second year can drop seed, so pull up stray seedlings where you do not want them.
seasoned: Rotate parsley and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share the carrot rust fly and carrot weevil, aster yellows, Septoria leaf spot, and soilborne crown and root rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow parsley with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because parsley is biennial and self-sows from second-year plants left to flower, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place.

beginner: Good news: parsley does not bolt in hot weather like cilantro does. It is a biennial, which means it grows leaves the first year and only sends up a flower stalk in its second spring, after a winter, when the leaves turn bitter. You cannot stop that second-year flowering, so the simple plan is to plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. Take a few early leaves from an overwintered plant, then let it bloom for the bees and butterflies or pull it out.
seasoned: Unlike fast cool-season herbs, parsley does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat; it is a biennial that flowers in its SECOND year, triggered by the cold of winter (vernalization). The practical consequence is the opposite of cilantro: a first-year plant gives leaves right through summer, but an overwintered plant sends up a flower stalk in its second spring and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter. There is no preventing the second-year bolt, so the standard practice is to grow parsley fresh each year for the best leaves, enjoy a short early-spring cutting from an overwintered plant, then let it flower (the umbels feed pollinators and host swallowtails) or pull it. Flat-leaf types tend to overwinter and hold a little better than curly types.

beginner: Parsley flowers on a two-year cycle: leaves the first year, then a tall flower stalk the second spring after it has been through a winter. That is normal, not a mistake, and it is very different from cilantro, which flowers fast in summer heat. The flowers are great for bees and are food for black swallowtail caterpillars. Grow new parsley each year for the best leaves, and let a second-year plant bloom if you want to feed the pollinators.
seasoned: Bolting in parsley is a biennial life-cycle event, not a heat response: the plant banks energy in a taproot the first year, overwinters, and flowers the second spring after vernalization. This is the defining contrast with cilantro, which bolts within weeks of warm weather. So summer heat does not end the parsley leaf crop, winter does (indirectly), by setting up the second-year bloom. The white umbel flowers are excellent insectary plants and a black swallowtail host, and second-year plants self-sow readily, so a few are worth leaving for pollinators even as you start fresh plants for leaves.

beginner: Do not leave cut parsley out on the counter, where it wilts; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water like a little bouquet.
seasoned: Fresh parsley wilts within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days, like cut flowers.

beginner: Store fresh parsley unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh parsley unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; it holds 1 to 2 weeks, longer than most cut herbs. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Parsley does not freeze well for salads, but you can chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze that for cooking. Drying works but loses a lot of flavor, so freezing is usually better.
seasoned: Parsley loses crispness frozen for raw use but freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or blended into sauces, holding its flavor for cooking. Drying is the weakest option: dried parsley loses much of its flavor, so freezing is preferred for preserving.

beginner: The best way to store parsley is to leave it growing and cut what you need. Picked parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks in the fridge. To save extra, freeze it chopped into ice-cube trays rather than drying it, since drying loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Parsley is best fresh from the garden and, because the plant keeps producing, the easiest storage is simply to cut it as needed. Cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks refrigerated, longer than most herbs. For longer keeping, freeze it (chopped in cubes or in sauces) rather than drying, which sacrifices most of the flavor; the University of Minnesota notes much flavor is lost in drying or freezing, so use preserved parsley within a year.

beginner: Pick the type for how you cook. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley like Italian Flat Leaf or Giant of Italy has the most flavor and is best for cooking. Curly parsley like Forest Green or Moss Curled is the frilly kind used for garnish and looks nice in pots. There is also Hamburg or root parsley, grown for an edible root. They all grow the same way, so just keep the soil moist and plant fresh each year.
seasoned: Choose by use. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley, including Italian Flat Leaf and Giant of Italy, has the strongest, sweetest flavor, taller open plants, and slightly better heat and overwintering tolerance, and is the cook's choice. Curly (French) parsley, such as Forest Green and the Moss Curled and Triple Curled strains, gives the dense, frilly leaves used for garnish and edging, with a milder flavor. Hamburg or root parsley is a distinct type grown for an edible parsnip-like root as well as leaves and wants deep, loose soil. All are grown the same way; variety matters less than steady moisture and fresh annual sowing, since any parsley bolts in its second year.

beginner: Parsley is small, leafy, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes in its second year: if you let it flower, the blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids on nearby crops, and they feed black swallowtail butterflies. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with asparagus, and with brassicas and onions. Keep it away from other carrot-family plants like carrots and celery, which share its pests, and from fennel, a poor herb neighbor.
seasoned: Much of parsley's companion value is real but indirect: a second-year plant allowed to flower is a strong insectary umbel, recruiting hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids on neighboring crops, and it hosts the black swallowtail. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which gain from those beneficials), with asparagus (a long-standing traditional pairing), and with brassicas and alliums that share its cool-tolerant culture. The well-grounded cautions are its own family, the Apiaceae (carrot, celery, dill, parsnip), which share parsley's pests and diseases and should be rotated apart, and fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor.

beginner: Let a second-year parsley plant flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and other pests. Parsley tucks neatly around the base of taller plants.
seasoned: A beneficial-insect and space pairing: parsley allowed to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids on tomatoes and peppers, and the low parsley fills the ground around the taller crops. Sound by mechanism and traditional practice, not a measured parsley-tomato effect.

beginner: Parsley and asparagus are a classic old-time pairing: parsley grows happily in the same long-lived bed and is said to help asparagus, and the asparagus ferns give parsley a little light shade.
seasoned: A traditional perennial-bed pairing: parsley is long associated with asparagus in companion lore, and practically the two share a permanent bed where parsley uses the ground between asparagus crowns and gets light shade from the ferns. Widely taught tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Cabbage-family plants and onions grow in the same cool weather as parsley and share a bed well, and parsley's flowers (in year two) help bring in insects that eat cabbage pests.
seasoned: A cool-season interplant on shared culture: brassicas and alliums share parsley's cool-tolerant season and bed, and a flowering parsley adds beneficial-insect pressure against aphids and caterpillars. Traditional and structural rather than a documented pairwise effect.

beginner: Keep parsley away from carrots, celery, dill, and parsnips. They are all in the same family and share the same pests and diseases, like the carrot rust fly and leaf spots, so growing them together builds up trouble.
seasoned: A same-family caution on shared pests and diseases: parsley, carrot, celery, dill, and parsnip share the carrot rust fly, carrot weevil, aster yellows, and Septoria leaf spot, so clustering or following one with another concentrates that pressure. Separate them in space and rotation. Extension-supported, not folklore.

beginner: Keep parsley away from fennel. Fennel is a poor neighbor for most herbs and vegetables, said to release substances that hold back nearby plants, and it can cross-pollinate carrot-family plants if both flower.
seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and the classic bad herb neighbor, releasing compounds that suppress many plants, and as a fellow Apiaceae it can cross-pollinate parsley where both flower. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured parsley-fennel trial.

beginner: The first thin little leaves poking up. Parsley is slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
seasoned: The first pair of narrow seed leaves pushing up. Parsley is famously slow and erratic to germinate, often 2 to 5 weeks, and emergence is uneven even under good conditions.

beginner: Soak the seeds before planting and keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings appear, which can take several weeks. Do not give up, parsley is just slow.
seasoned: Soak the seed before sowing and keep the surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Cold, wet soil prolongs it and invites damping-off; do not give up too early.

beginner: Any sprouts yet?
seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: The first true leaves, the lacy parsley leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
seasoned: The first true leaves, the broad, divided lower parsley leaves. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.

beginner: Thin the seedlings to a hand's width or so apart, eat the little ones you pull, and keep the water steady.
seasoned: Thin to about 6 to 12 inches as the plants crowd, eating the thinnings, and keep moisture steady while the taproot establishes.

beginner: How are they coming along?
seasoned: How are they coming along?

beginner: Leafy plants several inches tall and full enough to start picking the outer stems.
seasoned: Full, leafy plants 6 inches or more tall with several stems, ready to start cutting from the outside. This begins the long harvest.

beginner: Start picking the outer stems at the base now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming from the middle. A light feeding helps.
seasoned: Begin cutting outer stems at the base once plants are full; regular picking from the outside keeps tender new growth rising from the center. A light feeding here supports the long season.

beginner: Ready to start cutting?
seasoned: Ready to start cutting?

beginner: Full plants you can keep cutting from. Take the outer stems and the middle keeps growing new ones for a long time.
seasoned: Full plants you cut from continuously: take the outer stems near the base and the center keeps producing for months, right through summer and into fall, unlike fast-bolting herbs.

beginner: Cut the outer stems near the ground, no more than a third at a time, and it grows back. Pick in the cool morning. Parsley keeps going through summer heat that stops a lot of other herbs.
seasoned: Cut outer stems at the base, never more than about a third at a time, and the plant regrows all season. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor; parsley keeps producing through heat that would bolt cilantro or lettuce.

beginner: Parsley is a hardy herb in the carrot family, grown for its tasty, healthy leaves. It is easygoing once it gets started, and very different from both basil and cilantro: it handles frost and cool weather, but it also takes summer heat without flooding into flower the way cilantro does, so one planting gives you leaves from spring all the way through fall. The one tricky part is the beginning: parsley seed is slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks to sprout, so soak it in warm water first and be patient. You harvest it by cutting the outer stems near the base, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months. There are two main kinds, flat-leaf (Italian), which has the best flavor for cooking, and curly, the frilly kind used for garnish. One thing to know: parsley lives two years, and in its second spring it sends up a flower stalk and the leaves turn bitter, so plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. It has few pests, mainly the big green-and-black parsleyworm caterpillar, which turns into a black swallowtail butterfly and is usually welcome.
seasoned: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a hardy biennial herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae), grown for its flavorful, vitamin-rich leaves. Its biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil and the opposite of fast cool-season herbs like cilantro. Parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, taking light freezes and overwintering in mild zones, yet it is also genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: because it is a biennial that does not flower until its second year, it does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat the way cilantro does, so a single planting yields leaves spring through fall, and only the most extreme desert and subtropical summers slow it. That long, flexible season is the headline. The signature challenge is at the start: parsley seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, so growers soak it and wait. It is harvested cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems, leaving the center to regrow for months. It comes in flat-leaf (Italian) types, with the stronger, sweeter flavor cooks prefer, and curly (French) types grown for garnish, plus Hamburg root parsley grown for an edible root. The one catch is the biennial cycle: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so parsley is sown fresh each year for the best leaves. Pests are few, chiefly the parsleyworm (the handsome black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies) and aphids, and disease is minimal.

beginner: Start picking parsley when the plants are full and about 6 inches tall, a couple of months after sowing. Cut the OUTER stems near the base, no more than a third at a time, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months, even through summer heat. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and put it in the fridge, where it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild areas a mulched plant can live through winter and give you a few early leaves, but it will flower and turn bitter that second spring, so plant new parsley each year for the best leaves.
seasoned: Begin cutting parsley once plants are full and about 6 inches tall, roughly 70 to 90 days from sowing. Harvest by cutting the OUTER stems at the base, taking no more than about a third at a time, and the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the center for months, right through summer heat that would bolt cilantro or lettuce, and into fall. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and refrigerate at once; cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild zones a mulched plant overwinters for an early-spring cutting, but take that as a bonus: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so sow fresh plants each year for the main leaf crop.
